items.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I didn’t meet him, but I heard Oscar Pettiford and several of the family bands, the older families.

ctx.x: They felt that New York was fast. It was fast. They just didn’t have the desire to stay there. There were a lot of opportunities there. They wouldn’t stay.
We think about the Marsalis family, but they only have a sextet.
Didn’t want to work Mom too hard.

items.title: Delfeayo Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Later on I studied with Slide Hampton for a little while... But Slide, he showed me some harmonic things.

ctx.x: Let’s return back to your development as an instrumentalist. Who were your teachers in trombone, and who got you started on trombone?

I had a number of local teachers, mostly with the symphony. Greg Miller was in – in fact, he’s in the Louisiana Philharmonic still, but he was in the New Orleans Symphony then. And a couple of different guys. The names escape me. But I went to the Eastern Music Festival. I had Gregory Cox. He was with the – I think the Vancouver Symphony. So the symphonic trombonists have always been important to me. That’s where I developed my tone, my sound, and my appreciation for the sound of the trombone. Later on I studied…
Really? Let’s talk about studying with Slide Hampton and Curtis Fuller. That sounds . . .
